title: Match the piece, then the tops decide

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the top number of 3/8 turn from 3 to 6 while its shaded run stays put, so the tops, 6 against 5, agree with the runs, when you count both in sixteenths.
interactive.title: Count both in one piece
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Two one-inch bars, 3/8 above and 5/16 below, over one line. The stepper picks the piece both are counted in. Tops change, marks stay. New top = top × (new bottom ÷ old bottom).
interactive.ignores: Only pieces that measure both exactly are offered; eighths would leave 5/16 halfway through a piece.

explain.text:
To compare two fractions, count both in the same piece. 3/8 against 5/16: in sixteenths, 3/8 is 6/16. Six against five, so 3/8 is bigger, by one sixteenth of an inch. A shared bottom like this is a [[common denominator]].[^1]

The trap: 5/16 looks bigger because 5 beats 3 and 16 beats 8.[^2] But its 5 counts smaller pieces: 0.3125 against 0.375.

**Match the piece first; then the bigger top is the bigger fraction.**

analogy.text: A 500 mA fuse and a 3 A fuse: 500 beats 3 as bare numbers, but in milliamps it is 500 against 3000.
analogy.breaks: Units fix the piece for you; with fractions you choose it, and it must measure both.

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** same piece first, then compare the tops.

**Worked example:** the limit is 3/8 inch and the bit is stamped 11/32. 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so 3/8 is 12/32. 11 is under 12: the bit is within the limit.

**Common mistakes**
- Comparing tops while the bottoms differ.
- Choosing a piece that measures only one fraction.
